title: Angry at God
hook: the psalms, Job and Jeremiah all argue with God

segments.voice: Yesterday, strength in weakness: treasure in earthen vessels, and when I am weak, then am I strong. Your line was weak, then strong. Who did you tell about your weakness? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

A man sits with his feet locked in the stocks at a gate by the house of the LORD. He's been beaten for delivering God's message. The next morning he's let out. A few lines later in his book, the prophet Jeremiah turns to God and says this: "O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me." You tricked me, he says. You were stronger, and you won, and look where it got me. It's still there, kept in the scriptures of church and synagogue alike. Today: angry at God.

First, Jeremiah isn't alone. The Psalms have this edge too. Psalm thirteen opens, "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" Four times, how long. That's not a polite request. It's someone pounding on a door. And it was kept in the book the people of God sang together. Second, Job. A few days ago we met him and his friends. Before God ever speaks, Job says, "I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul." He keeps that promise for chapter after chapter. And he wants a hearing, not an exit: "Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat! I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments." He talks as if God's seat were a courtroom he's desperate to get into. Third, what Jeremiah does next. After accusing God, he says he'll stop speaking God's name altogether. And then: "But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay." He's angry, and he can't walk away. Anger at God, in these texts, can be a sign of how close the relationship still is. Some readers put it this way: you don't shout at someone you've stopped believing in. Last, what this means on an ordinary day. Some Christians were taught that anger at God is a sin to be hidden. These texts show another way: bring it, honestly, to the one it's aimed at. In the Psalms, that is prayer. He can take it.
screen: `JOB: I WILL NOT REFRAIN MY MOUTH.`
`A FIRE SHUT UP IN MY BONES.`
`BRING IT TO THE ONE IT'S AIMED AT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell God you're angry. Settle, and breathe. Is there something you're angry about that you haven't said out loud? An unfairness, a loss, a prayer that went nowhere, something done to you or someone you love. Let it come up. Don't tidy it. If you pray, you can tell God plainly, in your own words or with the psalm's: how long? If you don't pray, say it to the empty room, or write one honest sentence on paper. Then breathe, and notice that you're still here. The bell holds the time.
Angry at God. The honest fury of Jeremiah, Job and the Psalms, kept in scripture as a kind of prayer.
Your line: he can take it. Today, when anger rises, don't swallow it or throw it at someone nearby. Say it honestly, to God or on paper, first. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray the psalms of lament in services and alone, including their angry lines; some churches hold services of lament after tragedies, and pastors and spiritual directors encourage people to bring anger honestly to God in prayer.

myth: angry prayers were edited out of the Bible
Jeremiah, Job and Psalm 13 all argue with God, and they're still there.
Jeremiah's angry prayer comes after he has been put in the stocks
he is beaten and put in the stocks, let out the next morning, and then says, thou hast deceived me.
after accusing God, Jeremiah walked away for good
he tried to stop, but God's word was like a burning fire shut up in his bones.

fork.setup: you're Jeremiah. you've been beaten and mocked for speaking God's word, and you've just told God he deceived you. what do you do next?
options: quit, and never speak God's name again.
try to stop, but find the word burning in you so you can't hold it in.
fork.reveal: Jeremiah says he'll stop, then: his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones. angry, and unable to walk away.

trapdoor: what you thought: being angry at God means you've lost your faith.
what it means: Jeremiah, Job and the Psalms argue with God openly, and the Bible keeps their words as prayer.
what a scholar hears: Psalm 13 asks how long four times in two verses, then ends in trust. lament has a shape: complaint, request, and trust, all in one prayer.

notes: Job 7:11 begins 'Therefore I will not refrain my mouth'; quoted from 'I will'. Confirm.
'Before God ever speaks' for Job 7:11 is accurate (God speaks from chapter 38). 'Chapter after chapter' kept vague.
'Beaten and put in the stocks' from Jeremiah 20:2 (Pashur smote him and put him in the stocks). Confirm.
'How long' four times in Psalm 13:1–2 (KJV): counted in the cited text. Confirm.
'Read in churches and synagogues': Jeremiah is scripture for both; confirm the neighbor mention is acceptable.
'Anger at God, in these texts, can be a sign of how close the relationship still is' is interpretive; consider 'can be a sign'.
'Some Christians were taught that anger at God is a sin to be hidden' describes some teaching without naming any church; confirm fairness.
Day 1378 (Job again) covered Job's friends being rebuked; this day mentions it only briefly as part of a wider survey.
